facts.statement: Jobaria is the only known valid sauropod discovered in the Tiouraren formation.
facts.quote: Jobaria is currently the only known valid sauropod from the Tiouraren, where it was discovered in 1997.

facts.statement: Over 95% of the Jobaria skeleton is preserved, making it one of the most complete sauropods ever found.
facts.quote: With over 95% of its skeleton preserved it is among the most complete sauropods ever found.

facts.statement: The species name tiguidensis refers to the cliff of Tiguidi where the fossils were found.
facts.quote: The specific name tiguidensis comes from the cliff of Tiguidi, the site of discovery.

facts.statement: Re-interpretation of sediments suggests Jobaria lived between 167 and 161 million years ago during the Bathonian to Oxfordian stages of the Middle Jurassic.
facts.quote: However, re-interpretation of the sediments showed that they are more likely from the Bathonian to Oxfordian stages of the middle Jurassic in age, between 167 and 161 million years ago.

facts.statement: Jobaria was a primitive sauropod approximately 18.2 meters long and weighing about 22.4 tonnes.
facts.quote: Jobaria was a primitive sauropod, about 18.2 m long and estimated to weigh about 22.4 t.

facts.statement: In 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated Jobaria's length at 16 meters and weight at 16 tonnes.
facts.quote: In 2016 Gregory S. Paul gave a lower estimation of 16 m and 16 t.

facts.statement: Jobaria had a simple backbone and tail, unlike the complex vertebrae and whiplash tails of later North American sauropods like Diplodocus and Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Its backbone and tail were simple compared to the complex vertebrae and whiplash tail of the later North America sauropods Diplodocus and Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno suggested Jobaria could rear up on its hind legs based on comparisons of limb bone ratios with extant elephants.
facts.quote: It may also have been able to rear up on its hind legs as Paul Sereno concluded, after comparing the ratios of humerus and femur circumferences in Jobaria to extant elephants.

facts.statement: The classification of Jobaria is uncertain, with interpretations ranging from a basal macronarian to a non-neosauropod eusauropod.
facts.quote: The phylogenetic relationships of Jobaria are uncertain; it has been interpreted either as a basal macronarian, or as a non-neosauropod eusauropod, basal to the neosauropod clade.

facts.statement: Jobaria reached lengths of 21 meters, a height of 4.5 meters, and a weight of 18 tonnes.
facts.quote: Jobaria fue un saurópodo que alcanzaba los 21 metros de largo, 4,5 de alto y 18 toneladas de peso.

facts.statement: Jobaria had a short neck with only 12 vertebrae and large teeth.
facts.quote: Poseía un cuello corto con solo 12 vértebras y grandes dientes.

facts.statement: Jobaria's skull was made of fragile bones with a robust dome, large openings for the nose, and likely keen senses of smell and hearing.
facts.quote: El cráneo de Jobaria se constituye de huesos muy frágiles, con cúpula siendo la parte más robusta y tiene aperturas muy grandes para la nariz y los ojos tenían probablemente un sentido afilado del olfato y del oído.

facts.statement: Jobaria had a small, high, rounded skull similar to Camarasaurus, featuring a short snout, large nose, and spoon-shaped teeth.
facts.quote: El cráneo alto, redondeado es más pequeño y similar al del Camarasaurus, con un hocico corto y una nariz grande y dientes con forma de cuchara.

facts.statement: Jobaria's dorsal vertebrae were very simple, lacking air sacs and having simple spines.
facts.quote: Las vértebras dorsales son muy simples sin sacos de aire y espinas simples.

facts.statement: Jobaria had primitive limb proportions, with forelimbs not as elongated relative to the hindlimbs as in Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: Las proporciones de los miembros son primitivas, las patas delanteras no son tan alargadas con respecto a las traseras como sucede en Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: Jobaria was found in the Ingal bei Agadez region of Niger by an expedition led by Paul Sereno in 1999.
facts.quote: Jobaria fue encontrado en la región Ingal bei Agadez, Teneré, Níger por una expedición al desierto liderada por Paul Sereno en 1999

facts.statement: Multiple specimens, including an articulated adult and partial adults and juveniles, provide information on 95% of the animal, including clavicles and gastralia.
facts.quote: Se conoció por varios ejemplares, con un ejemplar adulto articulado y otros ejemplares parciales adultos y juveniles que juntos aportan información sobre el 95% del animal incluyendo las clavículas y gastralia.

facts.statement: The name Jobaria comes from "Jobar," a mythical animal of the Tuareg people who inhabit the Sahara desert region.
facts.quote: Su nombre proviene de "Jobar" un animal mitológico de los Tuareg, habitantes de esa zona del desierto del Sahara.

facts.statement: Originally, sediments were thought to date to the Early Cretaceous (Hauterivian to Barremian), suggesting Jobaria lived approximately 132 million years ago.
facts.quote: Originalmente se pensó que los sedimentos en los que se encontró representaban las etapas de Hauteriviano a Barremiano del período Cretácico temprano, lo cual dataría a Jobaria hace aproximadamente 132 millones de años.

facts.statement: Reinterpretation of sediments indicates Jobaria likely lived between 167 and 161 million years ago during the Bathonian to Oxfordian stages of the Middle Jurassic.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, la reinterpretación de los sedimentos mostró que es más probable que sea de las etapas de Bathoniense al Oxfordiense del Jurásico Medio, entre 167 y 161 millones de años atrás.

facts.statement: Jobaria has been interpreted as a basal macronarian by Upchurch et al. in 2004, or as a non-neosauropod eusauropod basal to the neosauropod clade.
facts.quote: Se ha interpretado como un macronariano basal por Upchurch y otros en 2004, o como un eusaurópodo no perteneciente al grupo de los neosaurópodos, siendo basal con respecto al clado de los neosaurópodos.

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Jobaria as Oxfordian to Tithonian (161.5 to 143.1 million years ago).
facts.quote: Time range: Oxfordian to Tithonian (161.5 to 143.1 million years ago)

rejected.quote: Discovered in the fall of 1997, during a four-month expedition to the Sahara desert led by paleontologist Dr. Paul Sereno
